::: {.oneline}
In equilibrium only the gap between two moments matters, so that one time
variable suffices, whereas once something has disturbed the system, when we look
matters as much as how long we waited.
:::

## Short answer

A system sitting in equilibrium has no clock. An experiment performed today and
the same experiment performed tomorrow give the same answer, so that the only
quantity which can matter is the interval between injecting a particle and
looking for it. One variable is therefore enough.

If we hit the system with a pump pulse, it acquires a clock. One hundred
femtoseconds after injection now means something different depending on whether
injection happened during the pulse, just after it, or long after the system has
relaxed. We consequently need two independent times, namely when the process
started and how long it ran.

It is convenient to reorganize these two into a different pair, that is, their
difference and their average. The difference behaves as it always did, since it
is what turns into a spectrum. The average carries the new physics, since it
tells us which spectrum, at which moment of the evolution of the sample. The
natural object out of equilibrium is thus not a spectrum, but a spectrum that is
itself slowly changing.

This separation only works when the two timescales are genuinely different, with
fast internal dynamics and slow evolution of the state. When the pump is as fast
as the dynamics it drives, an instantaneous spectrum is no longer well defined,
and the two times must be kept as they are.

## Why it works this way

The structure is the same as that of a spectrogram in acoustics. A steady tone
has a frequency, whereas a piece of music has a frequency changing with time,
which we describe with a sliding window. The window has to be long enough to
resolve pitch and short enough to follow the melody, and the tension between the
two is not a technical annoyance but the physics of the problem.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## The algebra: Wigner coordinates

Writing $t_1 = T + \tau/2$ and $t_2 = T - \tau/2$ and Fourier transforming on the
relative time $\tau$ only,

$$
G(T, \omega) = \int d\tau\; e^{i\omega\tau}\,
G\!\left(T + \tfrac{\tau}{2},\, T - \tfrac{\tau}{2}\right).
$$ {#eq-wigner}

In equilibrium the $T$ dependence drops out and @eq-wigner reduces to the
ordinary spectral function. Out of equilibrium, a gradient expansion in $T$
produces quantum kinetic equations of Boltzmann type, whose validity is exactly
the timescale separation described above.
:::

## Common confusions

- **"Two times is a technical complication of the formalism."** It is a
  statement about the system, since the loss of time-translation invariance is
  physical and not notational.
- **"The instantaneous spectrum is always meaningful."** Only when the state
  evolves slowly compared with the dynamics being resolved, since otherwise the
  transform can even go negative in places.
